question: The major focus of my recent travels has been visiting all of the UNESCO World Heritage sites. When I visit a new country, I feel like it helps me appreciate where I am staying for more than just a few popular sites I have seen on social media. I have been paying special attention to what they call "The List in Danger," and I like to prioritize those locations if possible. I have recently visited Cameroon and Chad, and I think that my next destination will be the Democratic Republic of the Congo in June 2025. While I am there, it is my dream to see a Kordofan giraffe. Where could I see them when I visit?

## Where in the Democratic Republic of Congo to spot a Kordofan giraffe | # | Location | Key facts | How to get there | Best time to visit | Practical tips | “List in Danger” status | Remarks | |---|----------|-----------|------------------|--------------------|----------------|--------------------------|---------| | 1 | **Garamba National Park** (NE DRC, near the borders with Uganda & South Sudan) | • The only place in the DRC where Kordofan giraffes (sub‑species *Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum*) live.
• Home to a recovering population: *≈ 100 – 120* giraffes (2024‑25 update).
• The park is a World Heritage Site (since 1983) *and* is on the “List in Danger.” | *By road*: Fly into **Goma** (ICAO : *FZJO*), the nearest major airport. From Goma, take a 4 × 4 tour (approx. 3–4 h) via the **Goma–Beni** highway to Garamba.
*By air*: Charter a helicopter from Goma directly into the park’s “Garamba airstrip” (if available). | **Early** or **late** July to September is the dry season – visibility is best and pig‑movement is reduced.
January‑March is also good but beware of occasional monkey‑borne disease risk. | • **Permits**: You’ll need a *National Park Permit* (purchased in Goma or via the park office).
• **Guides**: Trips are run by the **African Parks** management team or by local licensed guides.
• **Safety**: As of 2024, Garamba remains relatively safe compared to other DRC parks, but keep a copy of your embassy’s safety brief and be vigilant around the **Hole in the Wall** and rebel‑controlled areas.
• **COVID‑19**: Check latest health protocols; many tours require proof of vaccination or a recent negative test.
• **Cash**: Small‑change (USD/FCFA) – ATMs are scarce. | ✅ | • The Kordofan giraffe is the fastest‑growing critically‑endangered population of giraffes in the world. The park’s conservation success story is a major reason the park is on UNESCO’s “List in Danger.” | | 2 | **Kokombele–Garamba Corridor** (historical, adjacent to Garamba) | • This area forms the natural extension of the Garamba giraffe habitat but is **not a national park**.
• Access is limited; the Congolese Military and local militias control most routes. | • Generally **not recommended** for individual visitors unless you’re a researcher or part of an endorsed NGO. | — | — | — | • Mostly for conservation researchers; not intended for typical tourists. | > **Bottom line:** When you’re in the DRC, no place beats **Garamba National Park** if your dream is to see a Kordofan giraffe in the wild. --- ## Quick‐start guide for a Kordofan giraffe safari in Garamba 1. **Plan your travel window** - **July‑September** = Dry season, easier travel conditions. - Avoid **November–December** (heavy rains, roads become muddy). - If you prefer cooler temperatures, **January‑March** works well. 2. **Book a tour/caretaker** - **African Parks** runs a “Garamba Kordofan Giraffe Safari” (see their website: ). - They offer a **4‑day stay** that includes a morning giraffe drive, an evening wildlife walk, and an optional **camera‑trap session**. - Alternatives: NCH (National Council of the Congo) tourist desk in Goma can arrange a local guide. 3. **Getting there** | Step | Mode | Notes | |------|------|-------| | **Goma** | Flight | From Kinshasa (VIA Air Tanzania or SOAME) or from Nairobi/Entebbe (RwandAir). | | **Goma → Garamba** | 4×4 vehicle | 3‑h drive, with a step‑down to 4‑tire tires for rough roads. | | **Inside the park** | Foot/horseback | Site offers **walking tours** (up to 30 km) and **papo‑papo** overnight stays in a glass‑roof tent. | 4. **What to bring** - Light, breathable clothing + a hat. - **Binoculars** (10 – 20×). - **Camera** with a good zoom (12–16 ×). - **Sunscreen** (SPF 50+). - **Travel vaccinations**: Yellow fever, typhoid, meningitis, Hepatitis A. - **Mosquito repellent** with DEET. 5. **On the ground: you’ll see…** - *≈ 1/3* of the global Kordofan giraffe population. - Over 20 giraffes per group, usually traveling in maternal herds. - Complementary wildlife: forest elephants, leopards, hippos, and a diverse array of bird species. 6. **Respecting conservation work** - Keep distance (maintain 30 – 50 m). - No feeding or touching the animals. - Stick to designated paths to avoid damaging fragile vegetation that aids giraffe grazing. 7. **Support conservation** AD: Optionally **adopt a giraffe** through the Giraffe Conservation Foundation () or donate to African Parks. Your contribution helps maintain this “List in Danger” site. --- ## Why Garamba is listed as **“in danger”** - **Political instability**: The park borders rebel‑controlled zones (Lord’s Resistance Army, UPC). - **Poaching pressure**: While giraffe numbers have risen, other species – especially forest elephants and rhinos – remain highly threatened. - **Ecological threats**: Illegal logging and fishing encroach on critical habitat. Despite these challenges, Garamba has become a flagship conservation success story, proving that well‑managed protected areas can thrive even amid conflict. --- ## A bit of history - **Founded** in 1938, Garamba was the **first national park in DRC**. - The 1960s and 70s saw a dramatic reduction in giraffe numbers (from ~300 to ~100). - The **Giraffe Conservation Foundation** and **African Parks**’ re‑management began in 2016, resulting in a 5‑fold increase in giraffes by 2024. - Garamba is now a cornerstone of the **African Parks Conservancy**, a network of 7 parks across Central Africa. --- ## Other nearby attractions | Site | Why visit? | Distance from Garamba | |------|------------|-----------------------| | **Other DRC parks** (Maiko, Virunga, Kanun) | Fair world‑heritage protection; but these have very few giraffes and, often, higher travel risk. | 200 – 500 km | | **Lake Tanganyika** (south‑east of Garamba) | Unique freshwater biodiversity; long boat trips. | ~140 km south | | **Uganda’s Rwenzori Mountains** | Bird‑watching, trekking. | 200 km north | If you’ve already been in Cameroon and Chad, you’ve seen Garamba’s **kordofan** and **zapr** rangers keep wildlife safe; your next port will enrich that experience with live conservation working on the fence line. --- ## Quick FAQ | Question | Answer | |----------|--------| | **Is Garamba safe for tourists?** | Yes, but always stay with a reputable guide and check the latest embassy safety bulletins. | | **Do I need a visa?** | Most visitors enter under a tourist visa (or a *“Congo‑Visum”*). Apply at the DRC embassy/consulate. | | **What is the age of the Kordofan giraffe?** | They can live up to 25 years; the younger ones are the majority of the park’s population now. | | **Can I bring a child?** | Children (over 4 years) are allowed, but they may need additional mosquito protection and supervision. | --- ### Bottom line - **Garamba National Park** is the sole spot in the DRC where you can realistically see Kordofan giraffes in their native environment. - Plan a trip for the dry season, book a tour through African Parks (or the Congolese authority), and trend your travel itinerary with the park’s conservation status. - With a little preparation, you’ll walk alongside one of the planet’s most endangered giraffe sub‑species, while supporting a vital UNESCO “List in Danger” effort. Safe travels in June 2025 – you’re about to witness a truly remarkable corner of wildlife!

# Kordofan Giraffe Conservation in DRC
Garamba National Park in DRC is the last haven for the Kordofan giraffe in the country. Despite threats from poaching and rebel activities, GCF, African Parks, and the DRC government have successfully achieved a steady increase in giraffe numbers.

In the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Garamba National Park is home to the last remaining population of Kordofan giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum_), a subspecies of the northern giraffe (_Giraffa camelopardalis_). Established in 1938 as one of Africa’s first national parks, Garamba stood out for its uniqueness. However, its reputation has been marred by the activities of rebel insurgents (Lord’s Resistance Army) resulting in the loss of the last northern white rhino.
Over the past few decades, poaching has decimated the park’s wildlife, as rebel groups often resort to selling wildlife products to fund their illegal activities. Recognizing the dire situation, the Giraffe Conservation Foundation has collaborated with African Parks and DRC’s wildlife authority, ICCN, since 2016 to save the last natural giraffe population in the country.
Our collaborative efforts have focused on gaining a deeper understanding of population dynamics, habitat use, and immediate threats. The team of African Parks, with the support of the Giraffe Conservation Foundation, implements conservation monitoring and management activities through regular aerial and vehicle-based surveys to monitor all individually-identified giraffe.
The targeted giraffe conservation efforts have resulted in Kordofan giraffe numbers in the park and surrounding areas gradually increasing to over 100 giraffe. This positive trend underscores the importance of continued support for this crucial giraffe conservation initiative, which is slowly transforming into a remarkable success story.

[June 21](https://www.facebook.com/AfricanParks/posts/pfbid0E8rJ3budwDnp6fwUtuM5qmX2knzMEKhLrRCuNWfuCuTp4EKbQjiRTB5iSF74zyPFl?__cft__[0]=AZiopRnLjjKt_5tWDdaF6YnX5VeK9nmAIr6xTRrr2C0ADpUm2HySpXKZhe6IcwEk1IhTKpTx-SURpIpiCUNS63f8i4PbUj8_SYUerxPh39h5DFgd3D_gNz4nGVEd4U-cXY7xmnDw11iJncfsJ147cep5R5C8cTRE&__tn__=%2CO%2CP-R) ·
This World Giraffe Day, we’re celebrating the sheer diversity of Africa’s giraffe. The latest genetic studies show that there are four distinct species of giraffe (Masai, Northern, Reticulated and Southern), further divided into seven subspecies: Masai, Luangwa, Kordofan, Nubian, West African, Angolan and South African.

# African Parks - This World Giraffe Day, we’re celebrating... | Facebook
## African Parks's Post
We’re also mindful of the fact that only around 140,000 giraffe remain in the wild. Some of the key locations for giraffe conservation include [Garamba National Park](https://www.facebook.com/GarambaNationalPark?__cft__[0]=AZiopRnLjjKt_5tWDdaF6YnX5VeK9nmAIr6xTRrr2C0ADpUm2HySpXKZhe6IcwEk1IhTKpTx-SURpIpiCUNS63f8i4PbUj8_SYUerxPh39h5DFgd3D_gNz4nGVEd4U-cXY7xmnDw11iJncfsJ147cep5R5C8cTRE&__tn__=-]K-R) in DRC, and [Zakouma National Park](https://www.facebook.com/ZakoumaNationalPark?__cft__[0]=AZiopRnLjjKt_5tWDdaF6YnX5VeK9nmAIr6xTRrr2C0ADpUm2HySpXKZhe6IcwEk1IhTKpTx-SURpIpiCUNS63f8i4PbUj8_SYUerxPh39h5DFgd3D_gNz4nGVEd4U-cXY7xmnDw11iJncfsJ147cep5R5C8cTRE&__tn__=-]K-R) in Chad, which is home to around 50% of all the Kordofan giraffe in Africa. In South Sudan, Nubian giraffe appear to be thriving in wetland habitats where one might not normally expect to find them.

## Where in the Democratic Republic of Congo to spot a Kordofan giraffe | # | Location | Key facts | How to get there | Best time to visit | Practical tips | “List in Danger” status | Remarks | |---|----------|-----------|------------------|--------------------|----------------|--------------------------|---------| | 1 | **Garamba National Park** (NE DRC, near the borders with Uganda & South Sudan) | • The only place in the DRC where Kordofan giraffes (sub‑species *Giraffa camelopardalis antiquorum*) live.
• Home to a recovering population: *≈ 100 – 120* giraffes (2024‑25 update).
• The park is a World Heritage Site (since 1983) *and* is on the “List in Danger.” | *By road*: Fly into **Goma** (ICAO : *FZJO*), the nearest major airport. From Goma, take a 4 × 4 tour (approx. 3–4 h) via the **Goma–Beni** highway to Garamba.
*By air*: Charter a helicopter from Goma directly into the park’s “Garamba airstrip” (if available). | **Early** or **late** July to September is the dry season – visibility is best and pig‑movement is reduced.
January‑March is also good but beware of occasional monkey‑borne disease risk. | • **Permits**: You’ll need a *National Park Permit* (purchased in Goma or via the park office).
• **Guides**: Trips are run by the **African Parks** management team or by local licensed guides.
• **Safety**: As of 2024, Garamba remains relatively safe compared to other DRC parks, but keep a copy of your embassy’s safety brief and be vigilant around the **Hole in the Wall** and rebel‑controlled areas.
• **COVID‑19**: Check latest health protocols; many tours require proof of vaccination or a recent negative test.
• **Cash**: Small‑change (USD/FCFA) – ATMs are scarce. | ✅ | • The Kordofan giraffe is the fastest‑growing critically‑endangered population of giraffes in the world. The park’s conservation success story is a major reason the park is on UNESCO’s “List in Danger.” | | 2 | **Kokombele–Garamba Corridor** (historical, adjacent to Garamba) | • This area forms the natural extension of the Garamba giraffe habitat but is **not a national park**.
• Access is limited; the Congolese Military and local militias control most routes. | • Generally **not recommended** for individual visitors unless you’re a researcher or part of an endorsed NGO. | — | — | — | • Mostly for conservation researchers; not intended for typical tourists. | > **Bottom line:** When you’re in the DRC, no place beats **Garamba National Park** if your dream is to see a Kordofan giraffe in the wild. --- ## Quick‐start guide for a Kordofan giraffe safari in Garamba 1. **Plan your travel window** - **July‑September** = Dry season, easier travel conditions. - Avoid **November–December** (heavy rains, roads become muddy). - If you prefer cooler temperatures, **January‑March** works well. 2. **Book a tour/caretaker** - **African Parks** runs a “Garamba Kordofan Giraffe Safari” (see their website: ). - They offer a **4‑day stay** that includes a morning giraffe drive, an evening wildlife walk, and an optional **camera‑trap session**. - Alternatives: NCH (National Council of the Congo) tourist desk in Goma can arrange a local guide. 3. **Getting there** | Step | Mode | Notes | |------|------|-------| | **Goma** | Flight | From Kinshasa (VIA Air Tanzania or SOAME) or from Nairobi/Entebbe (RwandAir). | | **Goma → Garamba** | 4×4 vehicle | 3‑h drive, with a step‑down to 4‑tire tires for rough roads. | | **Inside the park** | Foot/horseback | Site offers **walking tours** (up to 30 km) and **papo‑papo** overnight stays in a glass‑roof tent. | 4. **What to bring** - Light, breathable clothing + a hat. - **Binoculars** (10 – 20×). - **Camera** with a good zoom (12–16 ×). - **Sunscreen** (SPF 50+). - **Travel vaccinations**: Yellow fever, typhoid, meningitis, Hepatitis A. - **Mosquito repellent** with DEET. 5. **On the ground: you’ll see…** - *≈ 1/3* of the global Kordofan giraffe population. - Over 20 giraffes per group, usually traveling in maternal herds. - Complementary wildlife: forest elephants, leopards, hippos, and a diverse array of bird species. 6. **Respecting conservation work** - Keep distance (maintain 30 – 50 m). - No feeding or touching the animals. - Stick to designated paths to avoid damaging fragile vegetation that aids giraffe grazing. 7. **Support conservation** AD: Optionally **adopt a giraffe** through the Giraffe Conservation Foundation () or donate to African Parks. Your contribution helps maintain this “List in Danger” site. --- ## Why Garamba is listed as **“in danger”** - **Political instability**: The park borders rebel‑controlled zones (Lord’s Resistance Army, UPC). - **Poaching pressure**: While giraffe numbers have risen, other species – especially forest elephants and rhinos – remain highly threatened. - **Ecological threats**: Illegal logging and fishing encroach on critical habitat. Despite these challenges, Garamba has become a flagship conservation success story, proving that well‑managed protected areas can thrive even amid conflict. --- ## A bit of history - **Founded** in 1938, Garamba was the **first national park in DRC**. - The 1960s and 70s saw a dramatic reduction in giraffe numbers (from ~300 to ~100). - The **Giraffe Conservation Foundation** and **African Parks**’ re‑management began in 2016, resulting in a 5‑fold increase in giraffes by 2024. - Garamba is now a cornerstone of the **African Parks Conservancy**, a network of 7 parks across Central Africa. --- ## Other nearby attractions | Site | Why visit? | Distance from Garamba | |------|------------|-----------------------| | **Other DRC parks** (Maiko, Virunga, Kanun) | Fair world‑heritage protection; but these have very few giraffes and, often, higher travel risk. | 200 – 500 km | | **Lake Tanganyika** (south‑east of Garamba) | Unique freshwater biodiversity; long boat trips. | ~140 km south | | **Uganda’s Rwenzori Mountains** | Bird‑watching, trekking. | 200 km north | If you’ve already been in Cameroon and Chad, you’ve seen Garamba’s **kordofan** and **zapr** rangers keep wildlife safe; your next port will enrich that experience with live conservation working on the fence line. --- ## Quick FAQ | Question | Answer | |----------|--------| | **Is Garamba safe for tourists?** | Yes, but always stay with a reputable guide and check the latest embassy safety bulletins. | | **Do I need a visa?** | Most visitors enter under a tourist visa (or a *“Congo‑Visum”*). Apply at the DRC embassy/consulate. | | **What is the age of the Kordofan giraffe?** | They can live up to 25 years; the younger ones are the majority of the park’s population now. | | **Can I bring a child?** | Children (over 4 years) are allowed, but they may need additional mosquito protection and supervision. | --- ### Bottom line - **Garamba National Park** is the sole spot in the DRC where you can realistically see Kordofan giraffes in their native environment. - Plan a trip for the dry season, book a tour through African Parks (or the Congolese authority), and trend your travel itinerary with the park’s conservation status. - With a little preparation, you’ll walk alongside one of the planet’s most endangered giraffe sub‑species, while supporting a vital UNESCO “List in Danger” effort. Safe travels in June 2025 – you’re about to witness a truly remarkable corner of wildlife!
